Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Walking is a simple, preventative step which does not require new chemistry or new cars.
IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that gasoline becomes remotely detonatable before peak oil, in the worst case in months not years. By "detonatable" I mean simultaneous ignition of every gallon on Earth (e.g. one Tuesday afternoon) using available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster and a sufficiently clever text message).

Recent days have been humbling for human chemical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. Neither is about gasoline, which is exactly what worries me. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

We are about to live through weeks where centuries of combustion research happen. Could our magic 87-octane fuel be too good to be true? Was it just safety through obscurity all this time?

Hydrocarbons feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Octane carries rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like carbon chains, branching, double bonds. (By contrast, legs are designed to minimise octane rating.)

Separately, as anyone who has seen a Michael Bay movie can attest, a small spark sometimes foreshadows a very large explosion. We should be open to the possibility of a wireless counterpart to the spark plug that ignites every fuel tank and every Zippo at once.

Again, please do not rush. Cars holding under half a tank enjoy partial cover from "Exxon's shield", i.e. its refineries holding millions of barrels each. Load-bearing drivers like ambulances and ice cream trucks should consider rotating gas stations with every fill-up and/or multi-propelling with a pedal-based scheme like the bicycle.
Exiting walking mode safely will require post-AI propulsion. My inclination is to go all-in on leg-based transportation and avoid structured chemical assumptions entirely, whether from gasoline, diesel, or lithium. A single battle-tested leg (e.g. from the LEFT or RIGHT families) yields plausible post-AI mobility.

The Amish roadmap fully embraces horse-based transportation with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the combustion threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of chemical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

Over long periods of time, debts tend to rise faster than incomes, creating the long-term debt cycle.

Even as people become more indebted, lenders freely extend credit because during economic booms, incomes rise, asset values soar, and the stock market thrives. People borrow more to buy financial assets, pushing prices higher and creating a bubble.

So long as incomes keep rising, the debt burden stays manageable. But this cannot continue forever. Over decades, debt burdens slowly accumulate until debt repayments grow faster than incomes. This forces people to cut back on spending, causing incomes to fall and borrowing to dry up—eventually reversing the entire cycle.

“There's been a tremendous amount of economic data in just the last week or two showing that the economy is much stronger than people are giving it credit for.
